{{Short description|Partial differential equation}}
In physics and mathematics, the '''[[Oskar Klein|Klein]]–[[Hans Kramers|Kramers]] equation''' or sometimes referred as '''Kramers–[[Subrahmanyan_Chandrasekhar|Chandrasekhar]] equation'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/kintheory/three.pdf |title=Stochastic Processes |last=Tong |first=David}}</ref> is a [[partial differential equation]] that describes the [[probability density function]] {{math|''f'' ('''r''', '''p''', ''t'')}} of a [[Brownian motion|Brownian particle]] in [[phase space]] {{math|('''r''', '''p''')}}.<ref name="Kramers1940">{{cite journal | last=Kramers | first=H.A. | title=Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions | journal=Physica | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=7 | issue=4 | year=1940 | issn=0031-8914 | doi=10.1016/s0031-8914(40)90098-2 | pages=284–304| bibcode=1940Phy.....7..284K | s2cid=33337019 }}</ref><ref name="Risken1989">{{cite book |first=H. |last=Risken |title=The Fokker–Planck Equation: Method of Solution and Applications |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |year=1989 |isbn=978-0387504988 }}</ref> It is a special case of the [[Fokker–Planck equation]].

In one spatial dimension, {{mvar|f}} is a function of three independent variables: the scalars {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|p}}, and {{mvar|t}}. In this case, the Klein–Kramers equation is
<math display="block">
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \frac{p}{m} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \xi \frac{\partial}{\partial p} \left( p \, f \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial p} \left( \frac{dV}{dx} \, f \right) + m\xi k_{\mathrm{B}} T \, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial p^2}
</math>
where {{math|''V''(''x'')}} is the external potential, {{mvar|m}} is the particle mass, {{mvar|ξ}} is the friction (drag) coefficient, {{mvar|T}} is the temperature, and {{math|''k''<sub>B</sub>}} is the [[Boltzmann constant]]. In {{mvar|d}} spatial dimensions, the equation is
<math display="block">
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{m} \mathbf{p} \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} f = \xi \nabla_{\mathbf{p}} \cdot \left( \mathbf{p} \, f \right) + \nabla_{\mathbf{p}} \cdot \left( \nabla V(\mathbf{r}) \, f \right) + m \xi k_{\mathrm{B}} T \, \nabla_{\mathbf{p}}^2 f
</math>
Here <math>\nabla_{\mathbf{r}}</math> and <math>\nabla_{\mathbf{p}}</math> are the [[gradient operator]] with respect to {{math|'''r'''}} and {{math|'''p'''}}, and <math>\nabla_{\mathbf{p}}^2</math> is the [[Laplacian]] with respect to {{math|'''p'''}}.

The '''fractional Klein-Kramers equation''' is a generalization that incorporates [[anomalous diffusion]] by way of [[fractional calculus]].<ref name="MetzlerKlafter2004">{{cite journal | last1 = Metzler | first1 = Ralf | last2 = Klafter | first2 = Joseph | title = The restaurant at the end of the random walk: recent developments in the description of anomalous transport by fractional dynamics | journal = Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General | date = 22 July 2004 | volume = 37 | issue = 31 | pages = R161–R208 | issn = 0305-4470 | eissn = 1361-6447 | doi = 10.1088/0305-4470/37/31/R01| url = https://cds.cern.ch/record/832337 }}</ref>

==Physical basis==
The physical model underlying the Klein–Kramers equation is that of an [[Damping|underdamped]] Brownian particle.<ref name="Risken1989"/> Unlike standard Brownian motion, which is overdamped, underdamped Brownian motion takes the friction to be finite, in which case the momentum remains an independent degree of freedom. 

Mathematically, a particle's state is described by its position {{math|'''r'''}} and momentum {{math|'''p'''}}, which evolve in time according to the [[Langevin equation]]s
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\dot{\mathbf{r}} &= \frac{\mathbf{p}}{m}  \\
\dot{\mathbf{p}} &= -\xi \, \mathbf{p} - \nabla V(\mathbf{r}) + \sqrt{2 m \xi k_{\mathrm{B}} T} \boldsymbol{\eta}(t), \qquad \langle \boldsymbol{\eta}^{\mathrm{T}}(t) \boldsymbol{\eta}(t') \rangle = \mathbf{I} \delta(t-t') 
\end{align}
</math>
Here <math>\boldsymbol{\eta}(t)</math> is {{mvar|d}}-dimensional Gaussian [[white noise]], which models the [[thermal fluctuations]] of {{math|'''p'''}} in a background medium of temperature {{mvar|T}}. <math>\boldsymbol{\eta}</math> is a row vector, making <math>\langle \boldsymbol{\eta}^{\mathrm{T}}(t) \boldsymbol{\eta}(t')\rangle</math> an [[outer product]]; <math>\mathbf{I}</math> is the {{mvar|d}} by {{mvar|d}} [[identity matrix]].
These equations are analogous to [[Newton's second law of motion]], but due to the noise term <math>\boldsymbol{\eta}(t)</math> are [[stochastic]] ("random") rather than deterministic.

The dynamics can also be described in terms of a probability density function {{math|''f'' ('''r''', '''p''', ''t'')}}, which gives the probability, at time {{mvar|t}}, of finding a particle at position {{math|'''r'''}} and with momentum {{math|'''p'''}}. By averaging over the stochastic trajectories from the Langevin equations, {{math|''f'' ('''r''', '''p''', ''t'')}} can be shown to obey the Klein–Kramers equation.

==Solution in free space==
The {{mvar|d}}-dimensional free-space problem sets the force equal to zero, and considers solutions on <math>\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{d}}</math> that decay to 0 at infinity, i.e.,   {{math|''f'' ('''r''', '''p''', ''t'') → 0}} as {{math|{{abs|'''r'''}} → ∞}}.

For the 1D free-space problem with point-source initial condition, {{math|''f'' (''x'', ''p'', 0) {{=}} ''δ''(''x'' - ''x''{{'}})''δ''(''p'' - ''p''{{'}})}}, the solution which is a bivariate [[Gaussian function|Gaussian]] in {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|p}} was solved by [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] (who also devised a general methodology to solve problems in the presence of a potential) in 1943:<ref name="Risken1989"/><ref name="Chandrasekhar1943">{{cite journal|last1=Chandrasekhar|first1=S.|title=Stochastic Problems in Physics and Astronomy|journal=Reviews of Modern Physics|volume=15|issue=1|year=1943|pages=1–89|issn=0034-6861|doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1|bibcode=1943RvMP...15....1C }}</ref>
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
f(x,p,t) =
      \frac{1}{2 \pi  \sigma_X \sigma_P \sqrt{1-\beta^2}}
      \exp\left(
        -\frac{1}{2(1-\beta^2)}\left[
          \frac{(x-\mu_X)^2}{\sigma_X^2} +
          \frac{(p-\mu_P)^2}{\sigma_P^2} -
          \frac{2\beta(x-\mu_X)(p-\mu_P)}{\sigma_X \sigma_P}
        \right]
      \right),
\end{align}
</math>
where
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
&\sigma^2_X = \frac{k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{m \xi^2} \left[1 + 2 \xi t -  \left(2 - e^{-\xi t}\right)^2 \right]; \qquad  \sigma^2_P = m k_{\mathrm{B}} T \left(1 - e^{-2 \xi t} \right) \\[1ex]
&\beta = \frac{k_\text{B} T}{\xi \sigma_X \sigma_P} \left(1 - e^{-\xi t}\right)^2 \\[1ex]
&\mu_X = x' + (m \xi)^{-1} \left(1 - e^{-\xi t} \right) p' ; \qquad \mu_P = p' e^{-\xi t}.
\end{align}
</math>
This special solution is also known as the [[Green's function]] {{math|''G''(''x'', ''x''{{'}}, ''p'', ''p''{{'}}, t)}}, and can be used to construct the general solution, i.e., the solution for generic initial conditions {{math|''f'' (''x'', ''p'', 0)}}:
<math display="block">
f(x, p, t) = \iint G(x, x', p, p', t) f(x',p',0) \, dx' dp'
</math>
Similarly, the 3D free-space problem with point-source initial condition {{math|''f'' ('''r''', '''p''', 0) {{=}} ''δ''('''r''' - '''r'''{{'}}) ''δ''('''p''' - '''p'''{{'}})}} has solution
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{p}, t) = \frac{1}{\left(2 \pi \sigma_X \sigma_P \sqrt{1 - \beta^2}\right)^3} \exp\left[-\frac{1}{2(1-\beta^2)} \left( \frac{|\mathbf{r} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_X|^2}{\sigma_X^2} +  \frac{|\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_P|^2}{\sigma_P^2} -  \frac{2 \beta (\mathbf{r} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_X) \cdot (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_P)}{\sigma_X \sigma_P} \right) \right]
\end{align}
</math>
with <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}_X = \mathbf{r'} + (m \xi)^{-1}(1-e^{-\xi t}) \mathbf{p'}</math>, <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}_P = \mathbf{p'}e^{-\xi t}</math>, and <math>\sigma_X</math> and <math>\sigma_P</math> defined as in the 1D solution.<ref name="Chandrasekhar1943"/>
	
===Asymptotic behavior===
Under certain conditions, the solution of the free-space Klein–Kramers equation behaves asymptotically like a [[diffusion process]]. For example, if
<math display="block">
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,p,0) \, dp \, dx < \infty
</math>
then the density <math display="inline">\Phi(x,t) \equiv \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,p,t) \, dp</math> satisfies
<math display="block">
\frac{\Phi(x,t) - \Phi_D(x,t)}{\Phi_D(x,t)} = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{t} \right) \quad \text{as } t \rightarrow \infty
</math>
where <math>\Phi_D(x,t) = (\sqrt{2 \pi t} \sigma_X^2)^{-1/2} \exp \left[-x^2/(2 \sigma_X^2 t) \right]</math> is the free-space Green's function for the [[diffusion equation]].<ref name="GanapolLarsen1984">{{cite journal | last1 = Ganapol | first1 = B. D. | last2 = Larsen | first2 = Edward W. | title = Asymptotic equivalence of Fokker-Planck and diffusion solutions for large time | journal = Transport Theory and Statistical Physics | date = January 1984 | volume = 13 | issue = 5 | pages = 635–641 | issn = 0041-1450 | eissn = 1532-2424 | doi = 10.1080/00411458408211662 | pmid = | bibcode = 1984TTSP...13..635G | url = }}</ref>

==Solution near boundaries==
The 1D, time-independent, force-free ({{math|''F'' {{=}} 0}}) version of the Klein–Kramers equation can be solved on a semi-infinite or bounded domain by [[separation of variables]]. The solution typically develops a boundary layer that varies rapidly in space and is [[Non-analytic smooth function|non-analytic]] at the boundary itself.

A [[well-posed problem]] prescribes boundary data on only half of the {{mvar|p}} domain: the positive half ({{math|''p'' > 0}}) at the left boundary and the negative half ({{math|''p'' < 0}}) at the right.<ref name="BealsProtopopescu1983">{{cite journal | last1 = Beals | first1 = R. | last2 = Protopopescu | first2 = V. | title = Half-range completeness for the Fokker-Planck equation | journal = Journal of Statistical Physics | date = September 1983 | volume = 32 | issue = 3 | pages = 565–584 | issn = 0022-4715 | eissn = 1572-9613 | doi = 10.1007/BF01008957 | pmid = | bibcode = 1983JSP....32..565B | s2cid = 121020903 | url = }}</ref> For a semi-infinite problem defined on {{math|0 < ''x'' < ∞}}, boundary conditions may be given as:
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
&f(0, p) =\left\{
\begin{array}{cc}
g(p) & p > 0 \\
\text{unspecified} & p < 0
\end{array} \right. \\
&f(x,p) \rightarrow 0 \text{  as } x \rightarrow \infty
\end{align}
</math>
for some function {{math|''g''(''p'')}}.

For a point-source boundary condition, the solution has an exact expression in terms of infinite sum and products:<ref name="MarshallWatson1985">{{cite journal|last1=Marshall|first1=T W|last2=Watson|first2=E J|title=A drop of ink falls from my pen. . . it comes to earth, I know not when|journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General|volume=18|issue=18|year=1985|pages=3531–3559|issn=0305-4470|doi=10.1088/0305-4470/18/18/016|bibcode=1985JPhA...18.3531M }}</ref><ref name="MarshallWatson1987">{{cite journal|last1=Marshall|first1=T W|last2=Watson|first2=E J|title=The analytic solutions of some boundary layer problems in the theory of Brownian motion|journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General|volume=20|issue=6|year=1987|pages=1345–1354|issn=0305-4470|doi=10.1088/0305-4470/20/6/018|bibcode=1987JPhA...20.1345M }}</ref> Here, the result is stated for the non-dimensional version of the Klein–Kramers equation:
<math display="block">
w \frac{\partial f(z,w)}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial}{\partial w}\left[ w f(z,w) \right] + \frac{\partial^2 f(z,w)}{\partial w^2}
</math>
In this representation, length and time are measured in units of <math display="inline">\ell = \sqrt{k_B T/(m \xi^2)}</math> and <math>\tau = \xi^{-1}</math>, such that <math>z \equiv x/\ell</math> and <math>w \equiv p/(m \ell \xi)</math> are both dimensionless. If the boundary condition at {{math|''z'' {{=}} 0}} is {{math|''g''(''w'') {{=}} ''δ''(''w'' - ''w''<sub>0</sub>)}}, where {{math|''w''<sub>0</sub> > 0}}, then the solution is
<math display="block">
f(x, w) = \frac{w_0 e^{-w^2/2}}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \left[w_0 - \zeta\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{G_{-n}(w_0)}{2nQ_n} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} S_n(w_0) G_n(w) e^{-\sqrt{n} z} \right]
</math>
where
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
G_{\pm n}(w) &= (-1)^{n} 2^{-n/2} e^{-n} (n!)^{-1/2} e^{\pm \sqrt{n} w} H_n\left(\frac{w}{\sqrt{2}} \mp \sqrt{2 n} \right), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \\[1ex]
S_n(w_0) &= \frac{G_n(w_0)}{2 \sqrt{2}} - \frac{1}{2n Q_n} - \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{G_{-m}(w_0)}{4 \left(m \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{m} n \right) Q_m Q_n} \\[2ex]
Q_n &= \lim_{N \to \infty} \sqrt{n!(N-1)!} \; e^{2\sqrt{N n}} \left[\prod_{r=0}^{N+n-1} \left(\sqrt{r} + \sqrt{n} \right) \right]^{-1}
\end{align}
</math>
This result can be obtained by the [[Wiener–Hopf method]]. However, practical use of the expression is limited by slow convergence of the series, particularly for values of {{mvar|w}} close to 0.<ref name="KainzTitulaer1991">{{cite journal | last1 = Kainz | first1 = A J | last2 = Titulaer | first2 = U M | title = The analytic structure of the stationary kinetic boundary layer for Brownian particles near an absorbing wall | journal = Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General | date = 7 October 1991 | volume = 24 | issue = 19 | pages = 4677–4695 | issn = 0305-4470 | eissn = 1361-6447 | doi = 10.1088/0305-4470/24/19/027| bibcode = 1991JPhA...24.4677K }}</ref>
